details:
Project Details – Space Relics: Stories Beyond Earth

Space Relics is an educational digital booklet that explores human-made objects remaining on the Moon and Mars after space exploration missions. It works by presenting four real examples and explaining their mission history, original purpose, and significance.

The project focuses on four objects: the Apollo 11 Lunar Module descent stage, the Apollo Lunar Surface Experiments Package (ALSEP), the Perseverance rover's backshell and parachute, and the Ingenuity Mars Helicopter. Each section tells the story of the object, explains why it remains on the planetary surface, and highlights what it teaches us about space exploration.

The main benefit of this project is that it makes space exploration easier to understand for students and the general public. It shows that objects remaining on other worlds are not necessarily useless waste. Some were intentionally left behind, some were released after completing their tasks, and others became historic artifacts after successful missions.

The intended impact is to increase public interest in planetary exploration, scientific research, and space technology. It encourages readers to look beyond famous astronauts and spacecraft and recognize the importance of the equipment and engineering systems that make missions possible.

The project was developed as a digital booklet using AI-assisted writing and document preparation tools. ChatGPT was used to help organize the content, structure the stories, and edit explanatory text. NASA's publicly available websites and scientific resources were used for research and fact-checking. No custom software, programming languages, or physical hardware were required.

The creative aspect of Space Relics is its storytelling approach. Instead of presenting space debris as a simple collection of abandoned objects, the project treats each object as a piece of history with its own mission story. It connects four different examples from two planetary surfaces to reveal how exploration leaves behind evidence of human achievement.

During development, we considered historical accuracy, scientific reliability, clarity, educational value, and the differences between intentionally deployed equipment and hardware separated during landing. We also aimed to use accessible language so that readers without an advanced scientific background could understand the information.

Space Relics ultimately demonstrates that the history of space exploration can be discovered not only by looking at what returned to Earth, but also by studying what remains beyond it.
